2. The petitioner, claiming to be a tenant holding land contiguous to the land sold in auction on 3-3-56 at a certificate sale, prayed for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The subject-matter of the pre-emption relates to the land recorded in R.S. Khatian 797 of Mouza Shahajira within police station Gournadi. 

 3. The auction purchaser opposite party contested the case traversing the material allegations and contending inter alia that the petitioner has no locus standi to pre-empt and as such his claim is not maintainable. According to the opposite party, he took delivery of possession through Court and is in possession of the land. He claims to have made improvement at a cost of about Tk. 8,000'00 within the knowledge of the petitioner. According to him the petitioner had knowledge of the auction sale from before and that the alleged date of his knowledge was not true and correct. The application was barred by limitation. It is further contended by the opposite party that he took delivery of possession through Court pursuant to the decree in title suit No. 388 of 1961 on 8-11-62 and that he has been enjoying usufructs through bargadars by cultivating the nal and bhiti land and also enjoying the fruits of fruit-bearing trees and the tanks by catching fish. According to the opposite party many persons holding contiguous land were not impleaded and as such the application was bad for defect of parties. It was further contended that the land in mainly a homestead, garden and tank and as such section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not applicable. 

 5. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed the decision of the learned Munsif and rejected the pre-emption application. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the application was barred by limitation. The learned Subordinate Judge did not believe the evidence of the P.Ws. Alauddin and A. Sobhan. According, to him these P.Ws. are not disinterested witnesses. The learned Subordinate Judge found that “it is the admitted case of the petitioner that the opposite tarty cut away trees from auction sold land, filed Title Suit No. 288 of 1961 against okhroit Bijoy Kumar and the latter filed criminal case against the opposite party so on and so forth. On the face of it, the case of the petitioner that he learnt about sale on 1-4-63 cannot be believed. It seems that the petitioner as owner to the contiguous holding had knowledge of the sale from the very beginning. "The learned Subordinate Judge on a consideration of the materials on record held that "the petitioner had no locus standi to file the case and that the case is not maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In reaching this conclusion the learned Subordinate Judge found that the case was one under the Bengal Tenancy Act but since the petitioner was not a co-sharer, he had no right to pre-empt under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. 

 6. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule contends that the pre-emptor had locus standi to apply for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred and accordingly the application was maintainable. That the sale was held on 3-3-56 and was confirmed on 5-5-56 and that the auction purchaser took delivery of possession on 5-6-66 are not disputed. According to the learned Advocate the right of pre-emption accrued not on the transfer but on the date of the pre-emptor's knowledge. That Part V of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in operation in the part of the district where the suit land situates is not in dispute. According to the learned Advocate since Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was in operation when the pre-emptor had knowledge of the transfer 'namely, the auction sale, the right of pre-emption as a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred was available to the petitioner by operation of law. It is not disputed that Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in force on 2-1-58 in that locality. According to the learned Advocate the whole period can be divided into two parts, one from 3-3-56 to 1-1-58 and the other from 2-1-58 onwards. During the period from 3-3-56 till before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was made applicable to the district, obviously, the petitioner had no right of pre-emption since he was not a co-sharer to the holding and during this period the candle of the Bengal Tenancy Act was burning. Thus, the right of pre-emption if any did not accrue in favour of the petitioner from the date of auction sale as contended by Mr. Rahim. He does not dispute that the auction purchaser's title to the land in question accrued on the date of sale i.e. on 3-3-56. If this branch of argument of the learned Advocate is accepted, the position comes to this that a right of pre-emption does not accrue with the transfer. Such an interpretation is not possible without violence to the language of the statute which runs as follows: 

 Thus, on a construction of the statutory provision quoted above, it is evident that the right of pre-emption does not accrue on the date of knowledge but on and from the date of the transfer. The period of 4 months referred to in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is the limitation prescribed for exercising the right by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred from the date of the knowledge of such transfer. Therefore, the petitioner had no right of pre-emption before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation. The right of pre-emption in respect of a transfer after Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation was available to co-sharers as well as tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred. A transfer before Part V came in force was open to pre-emption under the Bengal Tenancy Act although the application was made after Part V came into operation. In the circumstances there is no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate The petitioner had no locus standi to file an application for pre-emption as a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred in respect of a transfer which took place some two years before Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in force. Accordingly the application under section 96(1) at the instance of the petitioner was not maintainable. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge correctly decided the question on consideration of the materials on record and upon application of the law correctly to the facts and circumstances of the case. 

 7. It was next contended by Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, that the application was not barred by limitation. According to him the petitioner derived the knowledge of the transfer from Alauddin and Abdus Sobhan on 1-4-63. The learned Advocate contends that since the opposite party contended that the petitioner had prior knowledge, it was for the opposite party to prove positively that the pre-emptor had such knowledge in order to knock out the claim of the petitioner on the ground of limitation. I do not think 'there is any substance in this contention. The petitioner came to court to enforce a right. A period of limitation is prescribed by the statute for the purpose. The burden lies with him to prove the date of his alleged knowledge and that it is within the period of limitation. The pre-emptor is to succeed on the strength and proof of his own case. The learned Munsif, on consideration of the evidence on record made a clear finding that the petitioner was aware of the auction sale since before November, 1962 '" Reading the judgment as a whole, the irresistible conclusion is that the petitioner had knowledge of the auction sale since before November, 1962. The learned Subordinate Judge while concurring with the learned Munsif clearly found that: the petitioner as owner to the contiguous holding had knowledge of the sale from very beginning. In reaching the above finding the learned courts below considered the evidence of P.Ws. Alauddin and Sobhan. The learned Munsif disbelieved the evidence of Abdus Sobhan since he was over-zealous in support of the petitioner and went to the extent of saying what was "unusual". As regards Alauddin, the learned Munsif was of the view that he clearly stated in his evidence that he informed the petitioner after the acquittal of the criminal case which was on 12.8.63. The learned Munsif found that the story that the petitioner came to know of the sale for the first time on 1.4.63 from Abdus Sobhan and Alauddin is false." The learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the evidence of these two persons since they were not disinterested witnesses. 'As quoted earlier the learned Subordinate Judge observed Pit is the admitted case of the petitioner that opposite party cut away trees from auction sold land, filed T. S. No. 388 of 1961 against Okhrait Bijoy Kumar and the latter filed criminal case against the opposite party, so on and so forth. On the face of it, the case of the petitioner that 'he learnt about sale on 1.4.63 cannot be believed." Thus in view of the findings of the courts below on the question of the pre-emptor's alleged knowledge, the application is clearly barred by limitation. 

 9. On a consideration of the language used in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it further appears that the definite article "the" has been used to qualify “knowledge" occurring twice in the section. It, therefore, indicates that “the knowledge" must be definite knowledge. A precise or exact perception of the necessary particulars of a fact is the determinant of "the knowledge" which is essentially a question of fact. For the reasons stated above there is no substance in this application.
